strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing neural PDE solvers assume uniform time-stepping, which is impractical for high-speed compressible flows with shocks; the two-phase 'neural CFL + neural solver' framing is a sensible and novel decomposition.

Introduces several physically-motivated architectural ideas (CFL-inspired input features and max-pooling for the neural CFL model; Euler-residual and timestep-conditioned MoE strategies for the solver) that are grounded in classical numerics and prior neural-ODE/MoE literature.

Contributes two new, carefully generated supersonic CFD datasets (circular blast and multiphase coal dust explosion) produced with a validated high-order solver (HyBurn), with data and code promised to be released, which could be a useful community resource.

Extensive experimental sweep: 4 neural solver backbones (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, Transolver) x 3 timestep-conditioning strategies x 2 datasets, with multiple runs, standard errors, and physically meaningful evaluation metrics (correlation time, TKE error, mean-flow error).
Detailed appendices covering CFD problem setup, solver settings, training details, parameter/FLOP/memory counts, and many qualitative visualizations, aiding reproducibility and transparency.
weaknesses: The paper's central motivating claim (adaptive time-stepping yields more balanced training objectives and is beneficial relative to uniform time-stepping) is never empirically validated: there is no baseline comparing ShockCast against a neural solver trained/evaluated with fixed/uniform timesteps, so the core hypothesis is untested.

Results across conditioning strategies (Base/Euler/MoE) and backbones are inconsistent and do not point to a clear winning design; different metrics favor different configurations (e.g., U-Net+LayerNorm best for correlation time, but MoE/Euler with different backbones best for TKE or mean-flow), making it hard to derive actionable design guidance.

Some unrolled prediction errors are quite large (e.g., ~40-45% relative error on gas y-velocity for the coal dust explosion, and correlation-time-proportion of only ~60% overall for that dataset), raising doubts about the practical fidelity of the approach for genuinely turbulent/shock-dominated regions.

No quantification of actual computational speedup over the classical solver (the stated primary motivation for neural PDE surrogates in this domain), despite extensive discussion of FLOPs/parameters/memory for the neural models alone.

Limited empirical comparison to closely related adaptive/continuous-time neural PDE approaches mentioned in Related Work (e.g., TANTE, continuous neural fields, interpolator-based methods); these are only discussed conceptually, not benchmarked against ShockCast.

Evaluation sets are small (9-10 held-out cases per dataset), and both datasets come from a single solver/family of problems (2D, single code), so generalization to other high-speed flow configurations (3D, different solvers, hypersonic regimes) is unverified.

The neural CFL model's one-step MAE for the coal dust explosion case remains fairly high even with the best feature set (normalized MAE ~0.53), and it's unclear how errors in predicted timestep compound over long autoregressive rollouts beyond the single illustrative example shown in Figure 3.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and underexplored problem: adaptive (non-uniform) time-stepping for neural PDE solvers in the high-speed/compressible flow regime, where prior neural solver literature almost universally assumes uniform temporal grids.

Contributes two new, carefully generated high-speed flow datasets (multiphase coal dust explosion and circular blast) from a validated high-order CFD code (HyBurn), which could be a useful community resource if released as promised.

Reasonably thorough empirical study spanning four neural solver backbones (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, Transolver) crossed with three timestep-conditioning strategies (time-conditioned layer norm/spatial-spectral, Euler residuals, MoE) and several neural-CFL input/architecture ablations, with multiple training runs and reported standard errors.

Physically motivated design of the neural CFL model (CFL-inspired features, max-pooling as a proxy for the max-wave-speed operation in the true CFL condition) is a sensible and interpretable contribution.
Extensive appendices with qualitative visualizations, per-field error breakdowns, and an explicit limitations/future-directions discussion add transparency.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim of the paper — that adaptive time-stepping is beneficial for neural solvers relative to uniform time-stepping — is never empirically validated. No baseline neural solver trained/evaluated on a uniform temporal grid is included, so the actual benefit of the proposed two-phase adaptive framework over the much simpler uniform-step alternative used in prior work (e.g., [54, 55]) is asserted but not demonstrated.

No wall-clock or FLOP-based speedup comparison against the classical CFL-driven solver is provided, despite computational acceleration being the stated motivation throughout the introduction and conclusion; only relative errors and correlation-time metrics are reported.

Results across backbones/conditioning strategies are highly mixed and often the 'Base' conditioning (borrowed directly from prior work) is competitive with or better than the paper's proposed Euler-residual and MoE conditioning strategies (e.g., U-Net+Base wins correlation time in both datasets), undermining the argument that the newly proposed conditioning mechanisms are genuinely beneficial.

Absolute error levels remain fairly high in several settings (e.g., gas y-velocity unrolled relative error ~42-46%, TKE errors ~9-13%), and no comparison to any non-ShockCast baseline (e.g., simplest possible constant-Δt neural surrogate, or a naive interpolation baseline) is given to contextualize whether these numbers represent meaningful progress.

Evaluation sets are very small (9-10 held-out cases per dataset), limiting the statistical robustness of comparisons between many closely-performing model variants, especially given the already large error bars in Figures 5-6.

The technical novelty of the proposed conditioning strategies is somewhat incremental: Euler-residual conditioning is a direct reapplication of well-known neural-ODE/ResNet-as-integrator ideas, and the MoE conditioning is a straightforward adaptation of standard sparse MoE gating to be a function of Δt.

Despite framing the paper as introducing the first framework for temporal re-meshing/adaptive time-stepping, no empirical comparison (even qualitative) is made to closely related recent works discussed in Section 4 (e.g., TANTE, continuous-time interpolators, conditional neural fields), leaving the reader unable to assess how ShockCast's accuracy/efficiency trade-off compares to alternative approaches to the same underlying problem.
The dual-use/broader impact discussion (missiles, spacecraft, reentry vehicles) is only a few sentences and does not substantively engage with the implications.
